questions.question: Q: How was a Roman legion organised?

points.text: A legion had about 5,200 men, divided into 10 cohorts. Each cohort had 6 centuries of 80 men commanded by a centurion. The first cohort was double-strength. Auxiliaries (non-citizen soldiers) provided cavalry, archers and specialist troops. A legate (senior senator) commanded the legion with tribunes and a senior centurion (primus pilus) as deputies.

questions.question: Q: Why was the pilum an effective weapon?

points.text: The pilum had a soft iron shank connecting the heavy pyramidal point to the wooden shaft. On impact, the iron shank bent, preventing the enemy from throwing it back and making the embedded javelin drag down their shield, forcing them to discard it and fight unprotected.

questions.question: Q: How did Roman roads contribute to imperial control?

points.text: Roman roads (over 400,000 km total) enabled rapid troop movement across the empire, allowing quick response to rebellions or invasions. They facilitated trade, official communication (using relay stations) and cultural integration. The standard design (straight, well-drained, stone-paved) made them durable and efficient.

questions.question: Q: Why was Hadrian's Wall built?

points.text: Hadrian's Wall (begun 122 AD) stretched 117 km across northern Britain from the Tyne to the Solway. It marked the northwest frontier of the Roman Empire, controlling movement of people and goods, demonstrating Roman power, and separating the Romanised south from unconquered Pictish territory to the north.

questions.question: Q: How did the Roman army serve as an engineering force?

points.text: Legionaries built roads, bridges, forts and aqueducts as part of their regular duties. They constructed siege works (ramps, towers, battering rams) during campaigns. Standard overnight camps were built to a precise grid plan with ditches, ramparts and gates. The army's engineering capabilities were central to Rome's ability to conquer and control territory.
